profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting between the lead author of a survey paper and a postdoctoral collaborator to finalize the work plan for submitting 'MolGenSurvey: A Systematic Survey in Machine Learning Models for Molecule Design' to arXiv and a target journal special issue in six weeks. The context is that they already have scattered notes, a draft taxonomy, and a shared bibliography, but need to align on how to divide writing, consolidate coverage of recent papers, and define what the 'complete draft' should include before circulating it to two external coauthors. The agenda is to decide the survey structure, assign sections, set milestones for the literature pass and figure creation, and agree on what material will be included in the first full draft. The expected outcome is a concrete division of labor, a week-by-week timeline, and a shared understanding of what will be delivered at the internal draft deadline.

members.name: Dr. Lina Qiao
members.expertise: Molecular machine learning, scientific surveys, graph generative models
members.background: Lina runs a small ML for chemistry lab and has previously led two survey papers; she is strong at framing taxonomies, synthesizing literature, and managing publication timelines.
members.private_state: She wants a polished internal draft early enough to send to senior coauthors without looking underprepared, and is especially concerned about the paper appearing conceptually unified rather than just exhaustive.
hidden_assumptions: A 'complete draft' means prose-complete sections with placeholder citations resolved, figure captions written, and enough narrative polish to be shareable outside the immediate writing pair.
The 'recent work pass' refers to papers from roughly the last 18 months beyond the current Zotero library, because older canonical work is already sufficiently represented.
The taxonomy section naturally includes a short synthesis of downstream application areas only as framing, not a separate deep review of real-world deployment literature.
If someone is assigned to 'clean the bibliography,' that includes normalizing model family names and merging duplicate versions of the same work across arXiv and conference entries.

members.name: Dr. Mateo Singh
members.expertise: Benchmarking generative models, reproducibility reviews, chemical representation learning
members.background: Mateo recently joined the lab after a postdoc focused on reproducibility in molecular generation papers; he is meticulous about coverage and likes to build structured evidence tables before writing synthesis prose.
members.private_state: He wants to make the survey maximally comprehensive and citation-safe, and is worried about missing niche subareas or overstating trends before the evidence table is fully checked.
hidden_assumptions: A 'complete draft' means every planned section exists in skeletal written form with tables, bullet placeholders, and key citations, even if the prose is not yet polished.
The 'recent work pass' means a sweep of all papers since 2021 because the field changes quickly and many methods were first visible on arXiv long before formal publication.
The taxonomy section should extend to a substantive treatment of application settings and experimental practice, because readers expect the survey to bridge methods and use-cases.
If someone is assigned to 'clean the bibliography,' that means deduplicating references and checking metadata only; terminology harmonization happens later during editing.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the complete draft
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to have a 'complete draft' ready by the internal deadline.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means a prose-polished, externally shareable manuscript with figures, captions, and consolidated narrative transitions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means all sections exist with the right content and evidence structure, even if many paragraphs remain rough or list-like.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In academic writing meetings, 'complete draft' is a familiar phrase that often goes unexamined because both parties reasonably assume the other shares the standard used in their prior projects.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of the recent literature pass
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Mateo will do one more 'recent work pass' before the draft is consolidated.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this pass only covers papers missing from the current library, mainly from the last 18 months and a few obvious 2024 updates.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this pass includes re-checking the entire fast-moving modern wave from 2021 onward, including workshop and arXiv-first papers that may reshape section balance.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a routine finishing task rather than a major scope decision, so neither person thinks to define the date range or inclusion boundary explicitly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the survey should have an 'applications section' near the end.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a concise framing section that maps molecule design tasks to domains like drug discovery and materials, mostly at the level of motivation and open challenges.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a substantial review of domain-specific deployment settings, evaluation practices, and representative pipelines in each application area.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same high-level label and both think applications obviously belong in a survey, so the difference in expected depth hides beneath apparent agreement.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the bibliography should be 'cleaned up' before merging sections.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes cleanup includes unifying naming conventions across model families, merging duplicate citations, and making citation keys align with the paper's taxonomy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes cleanup is a metadata task in Zotero or BibTeX—fixing authors, venues, years, and duplicate entries—while terminology harmonization is part of later editorial revision.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Bibliography cleanup is usually treated as back-office maintenance, so each person silently imports their own workflow without signaling the hidden downstream implications for writing consistency.

turns.inner_thought: We only have six weeks, so I need the internal version to be genuinely shareable by week three, not a patchwork of notes. If I send something half-formed to the senior coauthors, it will look like I do not have the paper conceptually under control. Today I need us to lock structure and make sure the complete draft means a real manuscript with readable prose, figure captions, and resolved placeholders.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. Since we want the arXiv version and the special issue submission lined up within six weeks, I'd like to use this meeting to lock the section plan, divide ownership cleanly, and be very clear about what needs to happen before we call it a complete draft.

turns.inner_thought: The backbone is there already: representations, model families, objectives, benchmarks. What we still need is coverage discipline. Before we consolidate, I want one more recent work pass across everything from 2021 onward, including arXiv-first papers and workshops, because otherwise we could miss subareas that matter for claims about trends.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I think the notes are already in decent shape on representations, the main generative families, and task setups. Before we really consolidate, I'd suggest I do one more recent work pass so we are not locking in structure off an outdated snapshot.

turns.inner_thought: Good, one more recent work pass as a finishing sweep is fine, mainly to catch anything from the last year and a half that is not already in Zotero. I do not want that to balloon. More importantly, I want the complete draft by week three so I can circulate something polished enough that external coauthors are reacting to substance, not roughness.
turns.utterance: Yes, let's do that. And I'd really like the complete draft ready in about three weeks so we can circulate it internally without scrambling at the last minute.

turns.inner_thought: I should own the taxonomy because I already have the evidence tables and benchmark notes. And if the applications section sits with taxonomy, I can bridge methods to evaluation settings and how different subdomains actually use these models. Readers will want more than a short motivational wrap-up.
turns.utterance: In that case, I can take ownership of the taxonomy and the applications section. I've already been collecting notes on evaluation settings and benchmark usage across a few subdomains, so those pieces fit together pretty naturally on my side.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. He can handle the closing framing piece and tie the taxonomy to where these models matter in practice. I do not want that section to sprawl into a second survey, but as a bridge from methods to opportunities and open challenges, it should help the paper feel unified.
turns.utterance: That works well. I see the applications section as a nice closing bridge from the method categories to real-world opportunities and open challenges, so having it coupled to the taxonomy seems like a good fit.

turns.inner_thought: If I clean up the bibliography before merging, at least the shared library will stop causing friction. I mean standard metadata cleanup, deduping, venue details, years, author fields. I do not want everyone drafting against inconsistent BibTeX. Naming consistency can wait until prose editing.
turns.utterance: Also, before we start merging sections, I can clean up the bibliography so the references are in good shape when everyone is writing against the shared library.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, definitely. If the bibliography is cleaned up early, we can keep the model-family terminology aligned across graph, string, and 3D discussions and avoid duplicate citation variants creeping into the taxonomy. That will save editorial pain later and help the stitched sections read like one paper.
turns.utterance: Great, that will help a lot. Once the graph, string, and 3D sections get stitched together, having the bibliography cleaned up should make those model-family discussions read much more consistently.

turns.inner_thought: My order should be: recent work pass first, broad and systematic; then refresh the evidence table with method class, benchmark, and reproducibility notes; then write the taxonomy and applications section from that fuller base. If new papers shift the balance of what counts as established practice, I want that reflected before prose gets too fixed.
turns.utterance: So my plan would be to first sweep the newer literature, update the evidence table off that, and then draft the taxonomy plus the applications material from the expanded set.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take intro and the central synthesis because that is where the conceptual throughline has to be strongest. By the complete draft milestone, I want the visuals done too—taxonomy figure, comparison schematics, captions written—so the version we circulate already feels coherent and close to external-ready.
turns.utterance: On my side, I'll take the introduction and the core generative-model synthesis. And by the complete draft milestone, I'd like the figures and captions to already be in place so the whole thing reads as one manuscript.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine. For me, complete draft means every planned section exists, the tables are populated, and the structure is stable enough that polishing is a straightforward last pass. I do not need every paragraph to be elegant yet as long as the coverage and evidence base are all there.
turns.utterance: Yes, that seems reasonable. By then, all the planned sections should exist and the tables should be populated, which should make the later polishing pretty straightforward.

turns.inner_thought: For the week-two check-in, I want to see a tidy update rather than open-ended exploration: the recent work pass done, the bibliography cleaned up in the shared library, and an applications section outline that I can slot into the overall narrative. That should tell me whether we are still on track for a shareable internal draft the following week.
turns.utterance: Let's set a week-two check-in, then. Mateo, could you bring the refreshed recent work pass, the cleaned bibliography, and a draft outline for the applications section? That should give us enough to see how the back half of the paper is shaping up.

turns.inner_thought: That works. I'll have the broader literature sweep, the reference metadata in order, and a substantive structure for taxonomy plus applications. Once those are in the shared folder, we should have enough coverage to assemble the full draft quickly, even if some prose still needs smoothing afterward.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. I'll get those into the shared folder before the check-in, and once they're there we should be in a good position to converge pretty quickly on the full draft.
